PREFACE: ON THE TEACHING OF "LOCAL GOVERNMENT LAW" 

The ubiquitous yet often neglected course in "Municipal Corporations" or "Local Government Law" has long been with us in legal curricula. While the origins of the course remain in obscurity, a glance at the early casebooks will reveal a preoccupation with what might be called the private law of public corporations. How does the city enter into contracts? What are its property interests? What is its liability in tort?

To this extent, the course merely reflected the corporate legal responsibilities of organized communities. Up until the latter part of the Nineteenth 

Century, municipal concern with its environment was minimal, except for attention to housekeeping functions such as paving and maintaining city streets, providing a decent water supply, etc. Even here, as Earl Finbar Murphy's book on Water Purity has emphasized, municipal concern was sometimes negligent. In the field of water supply, for example, a good municipal system was often not in place until the stimulus of the 1930 depression forced an expanded program of public works.

With the rapid urbanization of the United States in the period immediately following the Civil War, and the consequent intensification of problems of city living, municipalities had to turn their attention increasingly outward, to the more rational control of their immediate environments. Tenement legislation in the 1890's, building codes, early gropings toward zoning and land-use controls, all were signs of the trend. Casebooks made room for these innovations. Chapters appeared which gave their entire attention to such subjects as zoning, without relating them to the total context of governmental problems and controls of which they were a part. As a consequence, a course which began with emphasis on the private, corporate aspects of municipal government turned from these internal concerns to a consideration of some of the external problems which communities faced when wrestling with their urban settings. As these changes in emphasis tended to occur ad hoc, the purpose and objective of the Municipal Corporations course blurred, with a corresponding and understandable lag in student interest.

Since the Second World War, the only major publishing event in the field of course books for local government has been the issuance of Dean Jefferson B. 

Fordham's casebook on Local Government Law (Foundation Press: 1949). The book had a profound impact on local government law teaching, and many of us acknowledge with gratitude the effects of the "Jeffersonian" revolution. Dean 

Fordham's book placed increased emphasis on the external problems of local government, expanded the range of attention to other units of government at the local level (hence the title), and for the first time included materials explicitly centering on the role of the state and federal governments in urban areas. Nevertheless, a continued division of emphasis between internal and external legal problems still marks the Fordham book. 

In the meantime, the increasing importance of governmental regulation of land use led to specific courses designed to cover these materials. On this subject, the pedagogical issues were raised in a debate at the L949 Annual Meeting of the American Association of Law Schools, where Dean Fordham and a distinguished panel of speakers argued whether land-use controls should be taught separately, in the property course, or in the course on local government law.

So far, the issue has been resolved all three ways, with the inclusion of land-use materials in some property casebooks and with the publication of independent casebooks on land-use controls.

fond J. 62 $4.7

ii These materials mark a more complete break with tradition in the teaching of that area of the law that has usually been assigned to "local government." 

They concentrate on the urban area and its problems, and not necessarily on specific units of government within urban areas. Of course, much of the content of these materials still falls in that area which can be designated "local government law." But the impact on our urban areas of potentially preempting state legislation, of state programs for highway and throughway development, and of federal-aid programs for urban renewal and other projects, cannot be overlooked. And this is certainly not a full listing of state and federal programs that have a local impact.

Secondly, these materials concentrate on the external problems of urban government, on the legal questions involved in managing and controlling the urban environment. In the more conventional sense, they combine the material that is usually covered in the course in land-use controls with material covering governmental power, structure, and organization that is usually found in courses in local government law. The merger is justified, however. Management of our urban environment is perhaps one of the critical problems facing Americans in the latter half of the Twentieth Century. Yet a resolution of this problem requires attention not only to the substantive content of controls over land use and re-use, but to the governmental structure within which these controls are exercised. To take one example, the formation of independent suburban governments is often spurred by a desire to control local zoning. 

This comment is an understatement. One commentator has referred to the zoning battles that go on in most suburban areas, as each community tries to dump its undesirable uses on the other. Even so, I might add, some important subjects have had to be left untouched. Air and water pollution the handling of natural resources in our urban community for the most part have had to be left for the comprehensive book which will cover these and other problems in the use of our natural inheritance. 

After an introductory chapter, the problems of delegating and sharing power are explored, not only in terms of Home Rule, but in terms of the impact of state and federal intervention and supervision. A long chapter deals with government in metropolitan areas, covering incorporation, annexation, and governmental reorganization. Dade County, Florida, is used as a case study. 

The final chapters deal with legal controls over the environment. After a discussion of the basis for intervention, and of the goals for intervention, the substantive materials are divided functionally into three chapters that deal with different areas of the metropolis city core, suburban fringe, and outer fringe. Within each chapter, programs of regulation and land acquisition which bear on the solution of environmental problems are considered in terms of each of these areas of the metropolitan community. The materials close with a case study on open space controls, which attempts to bring together some of the functional problems and doctrinal attitudes that have been discussed throughout. D.R.M.

CHAPTER I. THE PROBLEMS OF MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL: 

THE AMERICAN URBAN PATTERN A. The Rise of the Urban Problem 

On the eve of the Civil War, America was still a rural nation. There were few large cities; only twenty per cent of the population lived in urban areas. 

But a glance at the figures on the urban-rural distribution of the population indicates a steady increase in the urban sector from that time. From the Civil 

War to the turn of the century, the urban population doubled, although even by 1900 there were only three cities with a population of a million or more, and Los Angeles was a minor urban center of 100,000 people. 

In 1920, the per- Since that time, of course, the history is familiar. centage of population in urban areas first passed midpoint. By the 1960 census, about three-quarters of the population could be found in urban areas, and the trend shows no sign of abatement. Of most importance is the fact that virtually all of the population growth is going into areas that can be classified as metropolitan, ninety-seven per cent between 1950 and 1960 alone. 

California, with ninety per cent of its people in urban areas, thus becomes a prototype for the future image of America.

This vast population inherited a legal structure that was ill-prepared to receive it. American local government institutions, with the exception of New 

England, were based on a simple dichotomy of counties and municipalities. 

Counties are basically a rural entity without corporate status, and exercising judicial, tax-collection and related functions as delegates of the state. 

Municipalities are independently organized corporate entities with authority provide the basic housekeeping functions necessary to municipal existence. 

Even this function was not always well-performed. What Lincoln Steffens said of St. Louis in 1904 was typical of most great cities at that time: "The visitor is told of the wealth of the residents, of the financial strength of the banks, and of the growing importance of the industries, yet he sees poorly-paved, refuse-burdened streets and dusty or mud-covered alleys; he passes a ramshackle fire-trap crowded with the sick and learns that it is the City Hospital; 

Finally, he turns a tap in the hotel, to see liquid mud flow into wash-basin or bath-tub."

From The Shame of the Cities, p. 31 (1904), as quoted in Vernon, The Myth and Reality of Our Urban Problems, p. 4 (1962) In this and other respects, of course, the urban problem is not new: "If transportation is a part of the problem, as it surely is in anyone's analysis, we find evidence that the problem was acute for a considerable group of urban dwellers as far back as the early 

19th century. Before the Civil War, New York's downtown streets were already a jumble of brewery drays, horse trolleys, hackney coaches, and steam locomotives; * If housing is an aspect of the urban problem, then the urban problem again must be thought of as very old.

In the mid-19th century, every major city of the United States embraced teeming slums whose conditions of life were so incredibly shocking shocking even by the middle-class standards of the time --as to make the contemporary slum areas of East St. 

Louis and South Philadelphia appear benign by contrast. * If crime

From Vernon, The Myth and Reality of Our Urban 

Problems, pp. 2, 3 (1962) 

So it is not so much the newness of the urban problem, but an increase in its character and intensity which characterizes the first part of the Twentieth Century. At this point it would be helpful to identify some of the influencing factors in urban development that have wrought fundamental changes in the character of urban life, and that have put considerable pressure on the rural-urban, county-municipal structure of local government. (Townships are an intermediate level of government in many states, but their functions are distinctly rural and their role in metropolitan areas is minimal except in a few states, like Pennsylvania, which have conferred urban functions on township governments. But in these states they tend more to resemble a special district, a development in governmental form which will be discussed below). 

1) Rapidity of Growth. One of the real problems of metropolitan concern in the Twentieth Century has been the sheer increase in the numbers of people living in urban areas. Between 1900 and 1930, for example, population in urban areas more than doubled, and 38,000,000 people entered our cities. For the future, the prospect is even more staggering. By 1980 a population increase of over 80 million is expected, based on the 1960 census, and of this increase virtually all of it will go into metropolitan areas if present trends continue.

These staggering population increases have been more than our urban governments have been able to handle. Inadequacy of physical plant is one symptom, and in suburban areas the overcrowded school and the overflowing septic tank are symbols of a way of life more than the crack in the picture window and the two-car garage. The impact on land conversion has also been fantastic. Between 1950 and 1960, more open land was converted to urban use than had been converted in the prior 300 years of our history! Eand prices around urban areas reflect the pressure. Around Disneyland, in Los Angeles, residential land that had sold for $2,000 an acre in 1952 was expected to reach $16,000 an acre in the early 1960's. (The details are graphically presented in House and Homes's special August, 1960, issue on Land). 

More than that, rapid growth led to the rapid ossification of our governmental structure. Annexation laws had been provided in most states to permit cities to grow to include adjacent populations. But these laws were creaky, inadequate, and hedged about with restrictions. Nobody fully understands the reasons for the proliferation of suburban incorporated communities. But certainly one factor was the inadequacy of annexation laws. Another, of course, was the sheer inability of the legal process to keep pace with peripheral growth. In the mature metropolitan areas in the East and along the Great 

Lakes, our larger central cities were soon hemmed in by incorporated suburbs. 

As their populations aged, as younger families fled to the suburbs, central city populations started to decline. For many, 1950 was the high point. In short, rapidity of growth has been one of the factors that has led to the isolation of the central city, the flight to the suburbs, and the political balkanization of our metropolitan areas. 

2) Character of Growth. Location theory, an important new sub-discipline in social science, deals with the reasons underlying the location and growth of cities. In this country, most of our larger cities are the product of the 

Industrial Revolution. They grew to take advantage of natural resources, or of

a favorable transportation position. The necessities of commercial life led to the formation of the central business district, with its complex of stores and offices. Factories tended to locate at first in the inner areas, close to where their workers lived and close to rail transportation. Within the city, transportation was on foot, or later, by slow horse trolley. The streetcar and automobile revolutions came later. Our inheritance is thus a product of the early industrial age, an investment in fixed capital improvements which is hard to dislodge. 

Particularly in housing, the results are far from encouraging, and the inheritance of a poor housing supply has been one of the factors that has trapped large numbers of the deprived elements of our population in the central cities. As Vernon indicated, densely-populated tenements at high occupancies were a characteristic of urban areas from the very beginning. Into these came first the flood of immigrants from Europe Irish, Italians, Jews, and others. 

Most of them stayed in the slum for a generation and moved on, leaving behind, however, a residue of religious and ethnic groups who still tend to give character to the city. These early immigrants were joined by American cousins, young people from the farms and rural areas. Now the character of that American migration has changed, In 1910, 89 per cent of our Negro population lived in the South; by 1960, the figure had dropped to 60 per cent, and showed no signs of levelling off. By the 1960's, therefore, the isolation of the central city was accompanied by the slow building of a Chinese Wall between it and the rest of the metropolitan area. The central city was often Catholic, Negro, relatively poor, and Democratic. The suburbs were Protestant, White, relatively well-off, and Republican. There were exceptions, of course, but these deep divisions in the social fabric do not bode well for our urban. institutions. The Negro question underlies much that is wrong with our metropolitan areas today. Nobody would deny, for example, that the desire for an exclusive white neighborhood underlies much of the trend to suburbia; the writer could recount several instances in which the manipulation of suburban land-use and building controls has kept out even well-to-do Negro families. Particularly following the school integration decision, and the consequent integration of the schools in northern cities, many white families left the central city altogether, Whole neighborhoods, formerly held desirable, were deserted totally. In an interesting analysis of the racial problem, Eunice and George 

Grier find some provocative correlations, Not only have the Negro populations of major northern cities doubled and tripled in size, but the migration is spreading out. Syracuse, New York, for example, though starting from a small base, doubled its Negro population between 1950 and 1960. Furthermore, Negro birth rates are running ahead of their population ratios. In Washington, D. C., where Negroes comprise 54 per cent of the population, two-thirds of all births are Negro. (The Impact of Race on Neighborhood in the Metropolitan Setting, Washington Center for Metropolitan Studies, 1961). 

Washington is the first, but hardly the last northern city in which the Negro population has become a majority. At the same time, the Griers give us statistics which portray the Negro exclusion from the suburb. In a recent census survey of 32 suburban Chicago suburbs, only four had more than 100 nonwhites. (id, at 12,)

The problem is well put in a report of the United States Commission on 

Civil Rights: 

"Like earlier immigrants from overseas, many of today's largely native-born minorities have been forced into urban slums, restricted to the poorest schools, and employed in the lowest paid occupations.

Inevitably in their adjustment to city life under such handicaps, they have required a disproportionate share of health, welfare, police, and other services, and have been more vulnerable to personal and social maladjustment. As with earlier groups, these deprivations have led to discrimination, which in turn reinforces the deprivations.

While many of these problems are similar to those of other minorities, there are important differences. The Negro is no stranger to this country: he is an American by birth and by long ancestry. 

But he is set apart by the color of his skin. Moreover, many of his hardships are the bitter fruit of past denials of civil rights in this country. And the cumulative effect of these denials has produced a new deprivation debilitation of hope and ambition So that even opportunities that are available sometimes go unused. In contrast to the conviction of earlier immigrants that they their children could work their way up from poverty and slums, 'the outstanding characteristics of youth in the Negro slum is an almost complete lack of conviction that life can be better.'" 

or From Civil Rights, excerpts from the 1961 United States Commission on Civil Rights Report, pp. 8, 9 

Many A central The en- 3) Blighting Influences. Blight is the feature most characteristic of our central cities. Financial blight, social blight, physical blight. of the influences contributing to blight have already been sketched. city physical plant that is functionally if not physically obsolete. during and persistent character of our slum areas. And the migration of younger families and the relatively well-to-do to the suburbs, a process which began with the streetcar and commuter revolution and which has been accelerated by the automobile, and which has left the central city as an institutional caretaker for the deprived and the underprivileged. This state of affairs was noted by the Civil Rights Commission, which commented that social welfare costs in core cities have grown staggering as a consequence. At the same time, their housing and building stock continues to run down, their tax base declines, and their continuing deterioration accelerates the dispersal trend. sult is more low-income immigrants, even higher welfare costs, and an even lower tax base. The cycle is circular and vicious, and has been halted only slightly by massive injections of federal aid for housing and renewal. problem is summed up by the Editors of Fortune, in their exciting symposium, The Exploding Metropolis (1957): 

14 The re- "In the second decade of postwar prosperity, in a time of steadily advancing living standards, the slum problem of our great cities is worsening. Today some 17 million Americans live in dwellings that are beyond rehabilitation decayed, dirty, rat infested, without decent heat or light or plumbing. The problem is most severe in the biggest, richest, most industrialized cities. * [I]n all these cities and a great many more the number of people crowded into slums is growing faster than the population as a whole. block, the slums are spilling out into once respectable neighborhoods as the middle class leaves for suburbia." (p. 92.) Block by The 4) The New Mobility. But not all is well beyond the Chinese Wall. In the postwar era, not only the absolute and relative increase in automobile ownership, but improvements in automobile efficiency, in the highway system, and (perhaps as a result of these) an increasing tendency to use the automobile for longer and longer trips has created a suburban way of life different from anything we have known previously. Once more, the problem is one of

degree, and of the intensification of a suburban trend that could be detected as early as the 1880's. The issue is summarized graphically by Wilfred Owen: "In the days of horse cars and pedestrians, a radius of between two and three miles was comfortable commuting distance for the urban dweller, and the size of most cities was limited to about 20 square miles. Transportation by street car, railroad, and rapid transit lines later expanded the radius of urban movement to five miles, and the urban area to 79 square miles. In the more recent automotive age, however, a commuting radius of 25 miles and more has become feasible, and the automobile has made possible an urban area covering upwards of 2,000 square miles."

From The Metropolitan Transportation Problem, p. 32 (1956). 

Similar conclusions are reached in The Exploding Metropolis, a chapter on "The City and the Car" pointing out that in most major cities, except the very big ones, a majority of people enter the central business district by car. 

This chapter contains much original material on the costs and relative desirability of automobile transportation. It explodes some of the myths of public transportation, pointing out that the cost of driving an automobile is not all that much higher than the cost of going by bus. For this and other reasons, the difficulties involved in finding a way out of the transportation dilemma are by no means easy to overcome. 

But one developmental period impinges on another, and the automobile age has been replaced in turn by the expressway age. Beginning with the Highway 

Act of 1956, we accepted as a national goal the building of an Interstate and National Defense Highway network, spanning the country with thousands of miles of modern throughways that can hardly fail to change the character of the countryside. As one commentator has pointed out, the new highway system will shrink the United States by 29 percent. Nor should the impact of the new highways on our urban centers be overlooked. Our large cities serve as the control points for the Interstate System, the hubs in interlocking sets of spokes, and are ringed in turn by local offshoots of the highway system, bypasses and express highways which will enhance the opportunities for mobility in metropolitan centers. Our panaceas have so far seemed more a sedative than a cure, however. 

Expressways attract more traffic, congestion continues and grows worse, automobiles continue to pound into the city core, parking becomes impossible, and in some cities parking lots bid to become the dominant land use in the central business district. A recent survey in downtown Indianapolis indicates that streets, alleys, and parking areas take up 61 percent of available land in the original mile square! Whether the rebuilding of our metropolitan systems of public transportation is desirable or even possible is problematic. 

In this connection, the attempt of the San Francisco-Bay Area region to build a public system of rail transportation will be watched with interest. 

But the new mobility will have an even greater impact on what Lewis Mumford has called the urban grid. Commenting on his book, The City in 

History (1961), I noted: 

"We may have an urban grid sooner than we realize, for the completion of the interstate highway network will give us a lymphatic system with the interchanges acting as nodes around which new communities could sprout by the score. In Indiana, for example, the highway between Louisville and Indianapolis might conceivably be dotted

Changing Patterns of Living. 

Centralization of population in metropolitan areas was accompanied, beginning in the era after World War II, with the dispersal of metropolitan area population beyond the central city. The result is a change in American patterns of living which no one has explained satisfactorily, and which certainly is a product of central city deterioration, minority problems, increased mobility, and the desire for a suburban way of life. What happened has been well-described by Mumford: "The earlier type of suburb, which was most dependent on the railroad, had a special advantage that could be fully appreciated only after it had disappeared. These suburbs, strung along a railroad line, were discontinuous and properly spaced; without the aid of legislation they were limited in population as well as area. "What has happened to the suburb is now a matter of historic record. As soon as the motor car became common, the pedestrian scale of the suburb disappeared, and with it, most of its individuality and charm. The suburb ceased to be a neighborhood unit: it became a diffused low-density mass, enveloped by the conurbation and then further enveloping it." 

From The City in History, pp. 504, 505

What has happened, Mumford points out, is the destruction of the city. 

Suburbia is anti-city. Low-density, undifferentiated, mass housing has destroyed the spirit of community and the opportunities for interaction that were the basis of city life. Residential suburban development, in some areas occurring at densities as low as one-and-a-half homes per acre, is incredible when compared with the high densities of inner London or Manhattan Island. 

Mumford's description of Los Angeles "An undifferentiated mass of houses, walled off into sectors by many-laned expressways" is all too accurate as a description of many of our suburban areas. 

Nor is the American literature of suburban protest unfamiliar to most readers. Absence of the breadwinner, over-reliance on car and car pool, sameness of outlook, taste, class, and status, decentralization of leisure to the barbecue pit and the television set, all have been decried in turn. David 

Riesman puts it this way: "No, what is missing in suburbia, even where the quality of life has not overtly deteriorated, is not the result of claustrophobic conformity to others' sanctions. Rather, there would seem to be an aimlessness, a pervasive low-keyed unpleasure. * For millions of people, work no longer provides a central focus for life; and the breadwinner is no longer the chief protagonist in the family saga." 

From "The Suburban Dislocation" in Metropolis in 

Ferment, Annals of the American Academy of 

Political and Social Science, Vol. 314, p. 142 (1957).

ATRU COMEN

This brief survey of the development and nature of our metropolitan problem slums at the center, subtopia on the fringe has incorporated the conventional bases of modern social criticism. Both the slum and the subur ban way of life are deplored, the former on hygienic, the latter on social grounds. If these criticisms are accepted, the task of the lawyer is one of amelioration, of playing midwife to the legal and structural changes necessary to bring about a different urban pattern. And yet, in the face of continued criticism of both slum and suburb, the silence of their constituents is ominous. The alienation and deprivation of the slum dweller (it is not only a minority phenomenon) have already been described. But to this comment must be added the point that most slum dwellers do not view with favor the disturbances and adjustments that are necessitated by slum clearance and urban renewal; violent protest is the more common reaction. 

Nor do suburbanites appear distressed by their much-criticized way of life. To the contrary, the continuing acceleration of the outward trend would appear to confirm their approval. These characteristics of apathy and indifference were documented by Robert Wood in a speech to the 1962 National Con ference of the American Society of Planning Officials: 

"First, forays into the character of the urban public, their attitudes, opinions and dispositions for action, now depict a citizenry at best indifferent to the local political process. 

At worst our studies record postures of public frustration and alienation towards decision-making at the grass roots level. Scott Greer's 'suburban isolates! around St. Louis progressively withdraw their attention from public affairs to focus on family problems. * Murray Levin's alienated voter of Boston is a portrait of an electorate so sullen, skeptical and cynical that his political outlook borders on the neurotic. 

All these studies underscore the vast difficulties for modern local political leaders in mobilizing alert and continued public support. 

When they are put together with research documenting the decline of the local parties, the end of the powerful ward organizations and the demise of charismatic local political leaders, the prospects for expecting active civic participation in urban government seems low indeed. " 

From Planning 1962, p. 8.

This coursebook is organized on the assumption that the urban environment requires a reordering of the legal structure in order to rationalize a pattern that has produced both blight and chaos. To this extent, it accepts the conventional analysis of urban ills, and the traditional calls for change. 

Nevertheless, the indications of apathy and indifference give ground for раиве. In a society which puts so much emphasis on private satisfactions, the neglect of the public sector is inescapable. Under these conditions, the achievement of a consensus on community values is difficult. Why planners and urban commentators have set themselves opposed to the dominant trends in our society is a subject on which we might well ponder. But the lawyer should be aware of these divisions of opinion, and should well consider the impact of his role before he chooses sides. 

B. Community Response 

Community response to metropolitan ills has taken three general forms, and in none of these reforms has the lawyer played a particularly crucial role. Beginning at the turn of the twentieth century, with the exposures of 

Steffens and others, a movement for reform began which can be termed as the

-dox 

To od dial 

Now 

20

"neutralization" of the urban environment. Basic to this movement was the desire to take city government out of politics, which was found to be corrupt, and to put it in the hands of professional business "managers." The prototype of this kind of response was the city manager movement, which best represents the middle-class ideals of economy and efficiency which underlay much of this kind of reform.

Under the city manager plan the political element was to be removed completely, to the extent that the traditional office of mayor was eliminated. 

Even the role of the council changes. Though it continues to set local policy, under a strong manager form of government the manager will control all aspects of municipal administration, and will appoint department heads. 

Furthermore, the council is usually small, and is elected on a nonpartisan basis; in theory, the positions on the council are to be filled by lay citizens rather than politicians. While the council-manager plan has produced many good results, it has also produced problems. Central among these is the absence of a provision for policy leadership in the community. For this reason, the manager plan has usually been restricted to smaller communities in which a consensus about community problems already exists. 

With few exceptions, none of the larger cities, with real divisions of opinion over the drift of urban affairs, are governed by managers. 

Indeed, a growing point of view sees the problem of our really big cities as one of good leadership rather than good government. Again from 

The Exploding Metropolis (pages 63, 64): 

After speaking of the agressive big-city mayor, who has increasingly been elected to office in post-World War II years, the editors comment, "One of the biggest threats to his leadership, indeed, is too much 'good government.' The big problem at City Hall is no longer honesty, or even simple efficiency. * Today the big problem is not good housekeeping: it is whether the mayor can provide the aggressive leadership and the positive programs without which no big city has a prayer." A second important community response, which also developed in the early years of the twentieth century, was the movement for metropolitan governmental reform. As the large cities filled up and as their boundaries ossified, and as population spilled into adjoining areas, the same or similar middle-class groups that sponsored the clean government movement were also attracted to programs of reform in structure. In this case, again, the cry was often that efficiency and economy would result from the elimination of a multitude of governmental jurisdictions in metropolitan areas. On this point, incidentally, the experience of metropolitan government in Dade County (Miami) Florida is not encouraging. The satisfaction of pent-up service demands in that area has increased rather than decreased costs since the metropolitan government was organized.

In general, metropolitan reforms have concentrated on integration and giantism. That is, they have sought to integrate existing governments throughout metropolitan areas, with the substitution of a government vast in area and population in their place. What most characterizes the metropolitan reform movement is its conspicuous lack of success. Except for scattered cases of successful adoptions in places like Miami, Nashville, and Baton Rouge, the voters have soundly trounced most reorganization schemes wherever they have been presented. That this should be the result is not surprising in view of the outlook and expectancies of metropolitan dwellers. After all, the surburbanite left the big city in order to escape big city government. 

But the question arises whether decisions of governmental reform should be

left to the electorate. Refer once more to Wood's comment on voter indifference. Voter participation in elections on governmental reform has been negative, but it has also been low. Under these circumstances, does the election provide any kind of a consensus? 

At the same time, most suggestions for governmental reform have been based on a priori intuition rather than on any attempt to deal with the empiric problems of living together in a metropolitan area. Disagreement exists, for example, on those governmental functions that should be handled at the metropolitan level, and much of the argument that certain functions should or should not be treated as metropolitan in character is based on arm chair deduction. A good critique of the metropolitan reform movement is contained in Banfield & Grodzins, Government and Housing in Metropolitan Areas (1958). (See Chapter III.) In addition, many social scientists are dissatisfied with the emphasis on form and structure in government, and are concerned more with political behavior and with the ways in which governmental decisions are actually made. More cooperation may be possible, for example, between groups of suburban municipalities on the problems of fire prevention than between municipal departments that have charge of parks and streets, and whose interests may clash violently. A detailed attempt at a solution to problems of metropolitan government will have to await further development in these materials. However, two observations are pertinent at this point. Clearly a single, integrated government is not the solution for our very large metropolitan regions, some of which cross state lines. No single government, for example, could hope to cope with the governmental problems of the New York region. Adjustments more complex than those envisioned by the early reformers will have to be attempted in many areas. In addition, a persistent strain of thought in the literature on urbanism emphasizes the necessity of placing limits on city size. The case for restriction was put forcefully, in organic terms, in Lewis Mumford's latest book, and English planning and local government policy has in recent years been explicitly predicated on a restriction policy. If this is so, we may have to think in terms of a regional grid of inter-related communities, rather than in terms of a fully-integrated metropolitan region. The impact of the expressway network must once more be considered. 

A final community response to problems of metropolitan areas has been less consciously articulated, but has had important consequences nonetheless. 

I refer here to the shift of the balance of power in metropolitan areas to the state and increasingly to the federal level. Large-scale unemployment coupled with municipal insolvency in the 1930 depression stimulated extensive programs of federal public works under the New Deal. At first these programs were pragmatically oriented, and directed to the alleviation of unemployment and the provision of specific public facilities, such as municipal power plants and swimming pools. Low-rent public housing was also among one of the first federal grant-in-aid programs. Out of this start came a more comprehensive approach to the solution of urban problems, culminating in the federal Housing Act of 1949, and presently represented by the varied grant programs of the federal Housing and Home Finance Agency and its related departments. 

While monetarily the federal contribution to local programs has not bulked large, the programs of federal aid have covered areas of critical importance for the community, such as urban renewal, and so their impact has been greater than their financial contribution would indicate. 

In addition, federal statutes have imposed standards on the receipt of aid which, while first relating to the execution of the project, have been expanded to include

areas dealing with the planning if not the government of the metropolitan community. For example, at this writing federal aid for the acquisition of open space is conditioned on some form of cooperation among planning agencies in an "urban area. 11 And "urban area" has been defined broadly enough to include at least the territory covered by the Standard Metropolitan Statistical Area of the Census Bureau. Every indication points to increasing federal concern with structure and performance in urban communities. 

At the state level, while government has in many respects become merely a conduit for the flow of federal aid, to some extent state control over local government conduct has been increasing. State supervision over local financial responsibility is well established in states like Indiana and North Carolina. In other instances, regulatory functions at first exercised at the local level have slowly gravitated upwards. Public utilities regulation, liquor licensing, and the control of water pollution are three examples. addition, the imposition of state regulatory standards has tended increasingly to preempt local legislation. One example, not as well known as it should be, is the Uniform Motor Vehicle Code, which has had a substantial preemptive effect on local traffic ordinances. In The effect of increasing state and federal participation in local affairs is to alter substantially the balance of power at the local level. While a new equilibrium of federal-state-local relationships has not been established, attention to the balance of power problem should be one of the prime concerns of the local government lawyer. A counterpoint to the upward shift of power is provided by the Home Rule movement, which perhaps is the outstanding recent contribution of the lawyer to local government affairs. In opposition to the upward trend of governmental power, the Home Rule movement has sought to keep power at the local level. It seeks this aim by insulating local governments from state supervision and review and by carving out a legislative jurisdiction within which local communities can operate without state interference. Much misunderstood, and seldom wholly successfully, the 

Home Rule movement has a Victorian quaintness in an era of accelerating urban growth and metropolitan interdependence. Still, Home Rule forces show no signs of weakening, constitutional Home Rule adoptions have continued unabated, and the Home Rule concept is a force to be reckoned with. That lawyers would insert themselves in the political and governmental process at the very point where state restrictions on local government tend to bite most is matter of interest which will come in for more extended comment later. These materials will not deal with questions of internal organizational reform, which are outside the scope of our interest. They will definitely deal, however, with problems of metropolitan reorganization and the sharing of power at the local level. In so doing, they reflect the lawyer's historic concern for form and structure, a concern which many modern political scientists, oriented to a study of political behavior regardless of structure, have deemphasized. Nevertheless, problems of form and structure cannot be neglected altogether, and the case for the complete independence of behavior from form has neither been fully proved, nor alleged. 

C. Local Government in Metropolitan Areas. 

At this point it may be helpful to review the pattern of local government in metropolitan areas. While there is, of course, no "typical" pattern, neverthe less there are certain basic characteristics that can be noted and that are applicable regardless of area and location. Perhaps the best way to indicate these common characteristics is to take a metropolitan area of medium size, in the one million to two million range, and to indicate for it how governmental patterns have grown and developed, and what their present state of

Note should first be taken of regional variations in local government across the country. Here a distinction must be made between the relatively simple local governmental patterns in the south and in certain western states, and the more complex structures that are typical of the northeast, middle atlantic, and midwestern regions. In the south and parts of the west the county is the basic unit of government, there are no townships, and a relatively simple city-county structure makes governmental re-arrangement easier to accomplish. From Connecticut west to North Dakota and south to Kansas the city and township are the basic units, and while the township has tended to disappear in some states, in New Jersey, Pennsylvania and elsewhere it has been strengthened by the addition of urban powers. It is in these regions, especially in the states of the northeast and upper midwest, that the proliferation of townships and school districts makes the governmental structure more complex and more difficult to manage. Of some interest is the fact that our newest states, Alaska and Hawaii, have simple governmental structures few or no counties, no townships, few municipalities, state-run school systems, and few special districts. 

With these regional variations in mind, we can turn to the examination of local government characteristics in metropolitan areas. In a metropolitan area of the median size indicated there will, of course, be a central city, perhaps with a population in the neighborhood of a million or three-quarters million. It will exhibit the traits of blight and decline that have already. been indicated, and will be entirely surrounded by incorporated communities. (Often an incorporated community, like a cyst, will inhabit the city corpus.) 

In many cases, the framework for the metropolitan area will be a single county, although in an area that is over the million mark the commuting region will almost always extend over more than one county, and the probabilities are that the developed urban area will do so as well. Much will depend, of course, on the accident of location and geography. Milwaukee County, Wisconsin, for example, is narrow enough so that the band of development has now reached into Waukesha County, lying to the west. 

County government is rural government, and was never intended to be adapted to metropolitan concerns. Where the county has assumed metropolitan functions, as in Los Angeles, the change has been brought about by constitutional amendment or legislative enactment that has altered its character. 

Nevertheless, the county has the advantage of geographic comprehensiveness, and especially where it covers the entire metropolitan area it can become a convenient organizing focus for change. This was the experience in Miami, Florida, and Nashville, Tennessee. Nevertheless, the county has some disadvantages as a metropolitan unit. Its boundaries are frozen, either by constitution or by statute, and change may be politically impossible. In some states, county offices may be constitutionally enshrined, and change once more may be difficult. Finally, if the metropolitan area covers more than one county, as may likely be the case in the larger centers, the county "shell" cannot be used for innovation. One effect of county organization should be noted here. If the county does not have the authority to perform urban functions, there will be a power gap in unincorporated areas that may be quite harmful. In unincorporated, suburban Indianapolis, for example, there is no agency with the power to handle sewage and storm drainage. This power gap is one of the stimulants to suburban incorporation.

. Beyond the central city, interposed between it and the outer developing fringes of the metropolitan region, is the suburban layer. If the central city lies on a lake or major river, the suburban layer will fan out on three sides, although if it is on a river a metropolitan subcenter may coalesce on the opposite side and, just as likely, will be in another state. (E.g., Philadelphia--Camden.) Otherwise, the central city will be surrounded. porate similarities among suburban communities hides the fact that they are classifiable into several types, on the basis of function and age: Cor- Functional Types: Suburbs are usually divided into two functional types-bedroom suburbs and employing or "workers" suburbs. In America, the bedroom suburb is probably the prototype that comes to mind, although different patterns of living should not be discounted. In Paris, the wealthy live in the center and the suburbs are largely given over to the proletariat. Some bedroom suburbs are older, outlying communities that have been engulfed, and in these cases there may be at least the rudiments of an urban core, complete with a centralized shopping center that may have grown up at a crossroads. 

In other cases, however, especially in the case of those suburbs incorporated since the turn of the century, the suburban community may simply be a convenient chunk of the dormitory area that has been separated for governmental purposes. The true bedroom suburb will probably not even have a shopping nucleus, to say nothing of an industrial area, which the suburb may have incorporated in order to exclude. 

Employing suburbs often grew up around a railhead or junction point, attracting industry because of the convenience of transportation. The shift to trucking has made industry less dependent on rail transportation, so that the importance of the railroad as an urban focal point has diminished. A more modern movement, particularly prevalent in California, is the incorporation of an area including a modern industrial park in order to escape the burdens of taxation. In this category, the familiar example is the City of Industry, which was incorporated in the Los Angeles area. 

Of course, the bedroom and the employing suburb are extremes of type, and there are many in-between variants. Reference to the problems of taxation leads to a comment on financial capacity. Industry produces a substantial excess of tax revenue over fiscal need, and for this reason the employing suburbs tend to be tax rich. A heavy concentration of office and suburban commercial uses can have the same effect, as in the case of Clayton, Missouri. 

Bedroom suburbs, on the other hand, tend to be tax poor. Tract subdivisions built at high densities produce an excess of children over taxes, and especially in the newer suburbs the revenue gap prevents the community from keeping up with demands for educational, water, and sewage facilities. In Carle 

Place, on Long Island, the tax rate increased 278.2% between 1945 and 1955. 

This is an atypical case, but it represents a trend that is in evidence everywhere. 

Historic types: 

It may be helpful to differentiate suburbs further according to age. The older, interwar suburbs were usually built up slowly, at high densities, and according to a gridiron pattern. As they were adjacent to the cities, they usually constituted an extension of the older, built-up area. These characteristics, together with the slower rate of population growth and the more compact densities which antedated the motor age, allowed the older suburb to meet its service demands along with the increase in population. Today, the older suburb offers probably the most attractive bargain in the metropolitan community. Capital facilities are in place and paid for, blight is usually a worry rather than a reality, and the resident purchases convenience of access along with an older house that is usually twice as large as the modern ranch.

The modern suburb poses a different and more difficult problem. It is usually located in the second or third suburban layer, and lack of proximity to the central core may complicate its service problems. For example, it may not be able to contract for the extension of utility services from the central city. In addition, rapid growth at lower densities presents revenue and capital facilities problems that the older suburbs did not have to face. Lower densities increase the cost of capital facilities at the same time that the rush of population makes it that harder to keep up. A good example is schools. 

Low densities mean that the schools will be placed at greater distances, and expensive school bus services may be the result. 

Another important point to make is that the newer incorporated suburbs tend to be small and ill-conceived, with the result that the typical metropolitan area will be heavily balkanized into a jigsaw puzzle of small and inefficient local government units. In 1911, there were eight incorporated suburban communities in St. Louis County, which lies adjacent to and separate from the City of St. Louis. At the time of this writing there are 99, some of them no more than incorporated subdivisions. While twelve of the suburban municipalities contain about 75 percent of the county population, this fact makes the problems of government no less simple. 

Note: 

Additional discussion of the problems presented in this section will be found in Jones, "Local Government Organ ization in Metropolitan Areas: Its Relation to Urban Redevelopment" in The Future of Cities and Urban Rede velopment, pp. 479-572 (Woodbury ed. 1953), and in Adrian, Governing Urban America (2nd ed. 1961), especially in the beginning chapters. 

No account of local government in metropolitan areas would be complete without a discussion of the role of special districts. These can be classified into two types dependent and independent. Dependent special districts, such as some housing authorities, are fiscally and administratively the creatures of their appointing municipal authorities. Independent special districts, while perhaps called into being by a municipality, have fiscal and administrative autonomy in varying degrees. Statistics that often show the existence of several hundred governmental units in a given metropolitan area are blown up by the presence of a horde of special districts. (The 14 metropolitan areas with over a million people in each contain an average of 400 local government units apiece.) To begin with, education is almost always separately organized from the rest of the urban political structure, and the typical urban area will usually have at least a dozen independent school districts. The next most common variety is the independent single-purpose special district. These are most common in 

California, where a multiplicity of fire, lighting, and even mosquito abatement districts may be organized in metropolitan areas. One problem with the independent single-purpose district is its independence from fiscal and administrative control, and thus its relatively unregulated autonomy. Another is the district's inability to cope with the metropolitan service problem if it is organized at less than the metropolitan level. Services provided will vary unevenly from district to district, some areas will not be covered, and cooperation among districts will be lacking or inadequate. Another problem, of course, is that one special district or a combination of them is sometimes able to meet most of the service needs in fringe areas, thus cutting down on the attractiveness of annexation, or of some wider solution to the metropolitan problem.

3022

-- . In some areas, single-purpose districts are organized on a metropolitan basis, in which case they are able to provide adequate service at least for the individual utility which is covered by the metropolitan district organization. In this event, however, the problems of autonomy and independence are simply shifted to the metropolitan level, and the kingdom of Robert Moses in New York is a lesson to all of us. The trouble is that the metropolitan special district is seen in many areas as a complete solution to the metropolitan problem. In any event, while a metropolitan special district which would be multi-purpose and which would incorporate several functions would be useful, the tendency has been to stick to the single-purpose district as a solution. The reasons for this approach may not be too hard to discern, since the single-function district is easier to sell, and fits in easier with the existing professionalization and division of skills in the area of utility services. Furthermore, there are tax and revenue problems that are of prime importance. Special service districts can be financed by special assessments, service charges, functional taxes, and revenue bonds, all of which lie outside the municipal debt limit. 

When the local government pattern in metropolitan areas is surveyed as a whole, the result is a state of chaos that is well summarized in Meeting Metropolitan Problems, the 1960 Report of the California Governor's Commission on Metropolitan Area Problems: 

--In California, each new family requires approximately $13,000 of public expenditure to provide for its needs; 

-The property tax base in the City of Vernon, a tax-rich suburb, is one million dollars per person; in Los Angeles, it is $1600 per person; --In the Sacramento area, 25 local government jurisdictions have the authority to provide street lighting, but only a fraction of the area is lighted; --The cost of government services is greater in the suburban area than it is in the central city, but the quality of service is lower; --More than 2,000 independent governing bodies now function in 

California's nine metropolitan areas. (pp. 9, 10.)

We have been talking about the "typical," medium-sized metropolitan area. 

In the smaller, emerging metropolitan areas the problems may be less severe, to the extent that a majority of the urban population may still live in the central city, suburbs may not yet have sprung up on its borders, and annexation may still be possible and may be pursued with some degree of success. 

In these areas, there is still hope. On the other hand, the picture in the older metropolitan areas, located primarily along the eastern seaboard, is bleaker. There we have Megalopolis rather than metropolis, a band of urban development stretching from Boston to Richmond. There we have just begun to understand the complex interactions of metropolitan life, and there the solutions are still over the horizon. In Megalopolis, as local governments have matured, as blight has spread, as local government boundaries have ossified, the conventional solutions have appeared less and less relevant. What can be attempted is still a matter for conjecture, but some kind of regional solution, with a good deal of federal intervention, would appear to be the smallest conceivable dose of metropolitan medicine.

The Role of the Legal System. 

come, come Planners and architects design cities; lawyers, historically, have restricted them. Most local government law is relatively recent, the product of the middle and latter half of the nineteenth century, and most of it has been cast in the form of restrictions on what local government can do. Some examples are: Dillon's Rule, which restricts the scope of municipal powers; constitutional debt limitations, which restrict municipal borrowing power; the public purpose doctrine, which restricts the municipal spending power and, in a slightly different form, the eminent domain power as well. Even in the areas of incorporation of new municipalities and of annexation, what substantive law there is has been a law of restriction on what kinds of cities can be formed, and on what kinds of areas can be annexed to existing oommunities.

At the same time as a restrictive law of municipal corporations was being developed, a sovereignty theory of local government was adopted and then discarded. In a few states, notably in the Middle West, appellate courts of appeal toward the close of the nineteenth century announced a theory of an inherent right of local self-government. At first, inherent right theory was applied in situations in which the state legislature had interfered with internal city structure, but there were clear indications (and holdings) that it implied inherent legislative powers as well. While the old cases are still fondly carried in some casebooks, the inherent right doctrine was decisively dead in most areas by the middle 30's, the victim of increasing state concern with local affairs. Current doctrine recognizes the fundamental role of the sovereign state in our federal system. States delegated power upward to the federal government in the federal constitution. They also delegate power downward to local governments; their power, in this regard, is plenary. later discussion will show, the Home Rule movement has not been notably successful in altering this general position. As In a legal environment in which local governments were surrounded by restrictive doctrine and dependent for their legal existence and legal powers on the favor of the state legislature, lawyers had a critical role to play. 

But it was a negative one. By and large, it has been the job of the lawyer in local government to sound for the limits of local government action, and to delineate the areas in which government can and cannot act. He has, of course, been concerned with the revision of the framework where this has been needed, but he has not been temperamentally suited for the job.? 

The literature of local government law has largely been a compendium of existing doctrine. It has not tried very hard to project alternative models of structure and behavior, so that even those reforms that have been pushed the hardest have been a reflection of existing institutions. Perhaps this is why the Home Rule movement, which tried to work around existing restrictions on local authority, eventually was undermined by the very restrictions it tried to eliminate.

The bias of local government law toward the restrictive has been aided by the use of the judicial process as the institutional method for reviewing and controlling local government conduct and decision-making. Perhaps because of our constitutional inheritance, the conduct of governmental affairs in this country has always been characterized by the use of judicial review to set the limits of official behavior. This tradition contrasts sharply with the English, where local government at least has operated relatively free of judicial restrictions. Instead, the English have substituted a system of administrative checks and balances, and English local government is subject to thoroughgoing administrative supervision by a national ministry. While state administrative supervision of local government is increasing in this country,

no state has yet created a full-fledged urban affairs agency. Court review of local government is still the dominant pattern. 

The 

In assessing the value of judicial review as a control device, a distinction should be drawn between local governments as "agencies" of the state for the carrying out of governmental functions, and the more typical state and federal administrative agency that has adjudicatory responsibilities. adjudicatory agency is most clearly analogous to a court. One difference is that it operates under a statute which sets its substantive policy, but the constitutional issues surrounding these statutes have largely been settled and the application of their enabling authority is largely a matter for administrative discretion. Like a trial court, the adjudicatory agency decides "contested cases" involving adversary parties who dispute over a set of historical facts. The adversary process suits their needs, and while disputes rage over the amount of judicial review that should be afforded, the effectiveness of judicial review as a check on administrative action does not seem seriously to be in doubt.

Local governments themselves create adjudicatory agencies with the power to try contested cases. A good example would be a police board, with the power to try disciplinary cases. But when local government intervenes in the management of its environment, either in its own name or through an agency to which it has redelegated functions, the quality of its conduct and of its decision-making power take on an entirely different character. Concrete examples may make our meaning more explicit: 

1) The governing body may rezone a corner lot for a filling station; 

2) The urban renewal authority may condemn property in a blighted area; 

3) The board of public works may levy a special assessment for a street; 

4) The board of zoning appeals may grant a petition for a variance. 

Although each of these decisions may be made by different kinds of agencies, some of which appear to be legislative, some adjudicative, and some executive, these decisions have certain qualities in common which distinguish them from the more common type of adjudicatory decision by an adjudicating agency. These common attributes may be briefly described: 

While some of these 

1) Mixed legislative and adjudicative content. actions may appear to have a policy content (zoning amendment), and while some may appear to be adjudicatory of a set of facts (zoning variance), in each case the action taken is mixed in content. Those actions, such as zoning amendments, which are superficially legislative, may also deal with a very particularistic situation, such as a corner lot, and are therefore equivalent to a contested case over a particular set of facts. Those actions, such as zoning variances, which appear in the guise of adjudications, must always have a policy content to the extent that they affect not only the immediate parties but, in a permanent way, the shape and character of the environment. In 2) Ex parte character. In no instance is the proceeding truly adversary in that opposing parties contest for contrasting points of view of the same dispute. In some instances, the municipality initiates the action. others, much on analogy to utility licensing, an applicant seeks a municipal favor. Other parties may be permitted in the proceeding, but this may come later by way of judicial review. And if other parties do participate in the initial stages, as in a zoning variance proceeding, they appear as "friends of the court" rather than as adversary parties who must prove an opposing case.

Furthermore, in each of these cases, because of the impact of the governmental decision on the environment, there are larger community interests that may not be represented. 

3) Issues non-justiciable.

In each instance there is really no dispute over the facts involved, except in a very marginal sense. The problem, as in a case in which special assessments are being laid down, is usually the drawing of inferences from established facts. What benefits, for example, may be attributed to the paving of a street? Inferential deductions about environmental problems often present issues for decision that are not only complex but which raise questions of policy application that are not easily handled in the framework of adjudication. What, for example, is a community that is entitled to incorporation? When local government actions find their way into the courts for review and determination they thus present issues and problems that are not easily handled in the judicial process. These difficulties are reflected in the almost-universal judicial characterization of local government functions that affect the environment as "legislative". While this choice of language is hardly apt, the analogy meant is clearly to the "political question" doctrine of constitutional law. Like a political question, the issues raised by the exercise of "legislative" functions at the local level are not thought to be justiciable. At the least, the effect of this characterization is to limit the court's review function to peripheral matters. In almost all of the examples cited above, the action of the locality will be sustained in the absence of fraud or clear abuse of discretion. This position is the equivalent of the "scintilla" rule in administrative law, and the courts will sometimes say that they will affirm the local action if there is "any" evidence to support it.

While more extensive review might conceivably be available in a case, like a zoning amendment controversy, which raises a constitutional issue, even here the court's function may be limited. 

If there is any trend at all in the cases dealing with the review of local government actions, it is toward judicial abdication of responsibility in the exercise of the review function. This tendency is evident even in the zoning amendment cases, which really embody factual disputes in the context of a constitutional framework. A good recent example is: 

SMITH, Justice. 

ROBINSON V. CITY OF BLOOMFIELD HILLS 

Supreme Court of Michigan 

86 N.W.2d 166 (1961) Again we review a zoning ordinance. The property involved, located on 

Woodward avenue, in the city of Bloomfield Hills, is the former Hunter estate property. It is some 40 acres in extent and consists of a main building (of 

20 rooms and 8 baths) set back a substantial distance from Woodward avenue, and a number of smaller accessory buildings, all "typical *** of a passing era." 

It was purchased by Dr. Harley Robinson, one of the plaintiffs herein, in 1951. He desired to use it as a rest home but was informed that the property was zoned for residential use. Consequently, he applied to the city commission, the planning commission, and, finally, to the board of appeals for aid in his desire to use the property he had purchased as a convalescent home. "And you represented," he was asked, "to the members of the city commission and members of the planning commission that you had gotten into this

predicament through no fault of your own and it would be a hardship on you if you were not permitted to operate the property as a rest home?" The doctor answered in the affirmative. At any rate, whatever the pleas made, the board of appeals granted him what is described in the record as a "variance." acres. Thereafter Dr. Robinson conveyed to Brae Burn, Inc., a Michigan corporation of which he is one of the shareholders, a rectangular parcel of 14 This piece comprised the central part of the former Hunter estate property and included the main building heretofore described. In June of 1954 the corporation filed an application to enlarge the rest home (and remodel the barn) in order that additional patients might be accommodated. 

It was refused. A writ of mandamus was then sought by the corporation to compel the city of Bloomfield Hills, and certain officials thereof, to issue the permit theretofore requested.

There is a second suit before us (both cases were consolidated for trial). 

In the second suit, which is likewise for a writ of mandamus, Dr. Robinson (with Anna P. Robinson) and his present counsel, Arthur E. Moore, are the plaintiffs. They sought to construct a 3-story office building south of 

Brae Burn on Woodward avenue. Their application for a building permit was likewise denied upon the ground, in part, that the property was zoned as residential. The trial court, being of the opinion that the limitation on the use of the property was arbitrary, discriminatory, and unconstitutional, ordered that the writs issue in each of the actions. Upon leave granted, the defendant City of Bloomfield Hills took an appeal in the nature of certiorari.* In We are brought, then, to the merits of the zoning scheme itself. view of the frequency with which zoning cases are now appearing before this Court, we deem it expedient to point out again, in terms not susceptible of misconstruction, a fundamental principle: this Court does not sit as a super-zoning commission. Our laws have wisely committed to the people of a community themselves the determination of their municipal destiny, the degree to which the industrial may have precedence over the residential, and the areas carved out of each to be devoted to commercial pursuits. With the wisdom or lack of wisdom of the determination we are not concerned. The people of the community, through their appropriate legislative body, and not the courts, govern its growth and its life. Let us state the proposition as clearly as may be: It is not our function to approve the ordinance before us as to wisdom or desirability. For alleged abuses involving such factors the remedy is the ballot box, not the courts. We do not substitute our judgment for that of the legislative body charged with the duty and responsibility in the premises. Now as to the property before us and the ordinance before us: Much of the testimony taken went to the comparative value of the land if used for residential rather than commercial purposes. There is no doubt that its commercial value for [far?] exceeded its residential value. At the same time there is no doubt that even as residential property the land had considerable value. Thus one of plaintiffs' witnesses testified that the office building site was worth $32,400 for commercial use but only $15,000 for multiple dwelling use. The properties (Brae Burn and the office building site), we are told, "lie on Woodward Avenue, one of the busiest thoroughfares in the State of Michigan. They are natural business sites, ***." It is urged, from this and similar considerations, that "such zoning is confiscatory," that it is unreasonable, and that the property is not being put to its best use. Disparity in values between residential and commercial uses will always exist. 

In the leading case of Village of Euclid, Ohio v. Ambler Realty Co., 272 U.S. 

365,47 S.Ct. 114, 71 L.Ed. 303, Mr. Justice Sutherland, in upholding the ordinance, noted that the property involved was worth about $10,000 per acre

If such a showing serves to invalidate an ordinance the efforts of our people to determine their living conditions will be hopeless. To avoid "confiscation" in this sense (the obtaining of the highest dollar for one particular lot) will result in confiscation of far greater scope in property values in the municipality as a whole due to its inability to control its growth and development. It is argued, also, that nearby is found an office building (McManus, John & Adams, at the northwest corner of Woodward avenue and West Long Lake road), and that across the street is found another similar rest home. The se differences are bound to occur in any zoning plan. Somewhere one zone must end and another start. There will always be peripheral problems. But as the 

Supreme Court of Illinois expressed it in a recent "across-the-street" case 

(Wesemann v. Village of La Grange Park, 407 Ill. 81, 87, 88, 94 N.E.2d 904, 908): "It is practically a suburb of Chicago and is about fifteen miles to the west of the Loop district. The village authorities have been diligent in attempting to enforce its zoning regulations. It is the province of the municipal body to draw the line of demarcation as to the use and purpose to which property shall be assigned or placed, and it is neither the province nor duty of courts to interfere with the discretion with which such bodies are invested, except where there is a clear showing of an abuse of that discretion, which is not the case where the question is 

"The fixing of zoning lines is a matter of legislative discretion and necessarily results in a different classification of uses on either side of the line. This does not render limitations on use of property near the boundary line in a more restricted district unreasonable or invalid. " 

See, also, 1954 U. of Ill. L. Forum at p. 719; Babcock, 15 U. of Chicago 

L.Rev. 87. The function of the courts, with respect to these cases lies largely in two broad areas: (a) has the legislative body the authority to act? (b) have the requirements of administrative due process been observed with respect to adoption, interpresentation, and administration of the ordinance in question? The first brings to us the validity and breadth of the delegation of power.

The second brings to us the legality of its use, whether the ordinance was properly adopted, whether exercised as to all alike, regardless of local pressures and improper influences, and similar questions. These are the areas in which we may be presumed to have some degree of competence. But many of the cases coming to us involve merely the legislative judgment. They are the peripheral problems (should the line be drawn here, or there?) and the allegations of more advantageous use, with its corollary of "confiscation" (the property is worth more if devoted to some other use). Save in the most extreme instances, involving clearly whimsical action, we will not disturb the legislative judgment. It is immaterial that we, as legislators, would have been wiser. We are acutely aware of the doctrine of the separation of powers. A legislative determination within its sphere of government is conclusive upon us.

Comments: 1. A dissenting point of view is found in Vickers v.

Township 

Committee of Gloucester Township, 181 A.2d 129 (N.J. 1962). The township passed a zoning ordinance excluding trailers from its industrial districts, and the ordinance was sustained by the majority opinion. Two justices dissented in an opinion which reviewed the role of the judiciary in the review of zoning ordinances: 

HALL, J. (dissenting).

I am The majority decides that this particular municipality may constitutionally say, through exercise of the zoning power, that its residents may not live in trailers--or in mobile homes, to use a more descriptive term. convinced such a conclusion in this case is manifestly wrong. Of even greater concern is the judicial process by which it is reached and the breadth of the rationale. The import of the holding gives almost boundless freedom to developing municipalities to erect exclusionary walls on their boundaries, according to local whim or selfish desire, and to use the zoning power for aims beyond its legitimate purposes. Prohibition of mobile home parks, although an important issue in itself, becomes, in this larger aspect, somewhat a symbol. 

The instant case, both in its physical setting and in the issues raised, is typical of land use controversies now current in so many New Jersey municipalities on the outer ring of the built up urban and suburban areas. These are municipalities with relatively few people and a lot of open space, but in the throes, or soon to be reached by the inevitable tide, of industrial and commercial decentralization and mass population migration from the already densely settled central cores. They are not small, homogeneous communities with permanent character already established, like the settled suburbs surrounding the cities in which planning and zoning may properly be geared around things as they are and as they will pretty much continue to be. On the contrary these areas are sprawling, heterogeneous governmental units, mostly townships, each really amounting to a region of considerable size in itself. 

There present rural, semi-rural or mixed nature is about to change substantially and they are soon to become melded into the whole metropolitan area. 

Their political boundaries are artificial and hence of relatively little significance beyond defining one unit of local government. Their existing conglomeration of land uses is sectionally distributed--large or small scale agriculture, residences in separated communities and on good sized plots or acreage in the open country, business establishments in the populated sectors and along through highways, and perhaps a spot or two of industry much sought after to aid municipal tax revenues. Many differing land uses, both present and future, are and can be made comfortably compatible by reason of the distances involved and the varying characteristics of geographical sections. 

Present municipal services are not more extensive than necessary to serve a population scattered over a large territory. Increased facilities, especially schools, required to accommodate a sudden population growth of large proportions must be provided almost solely at local expense, which in New Jersey means from additional taxation on real estate within the municipal boundaries. 

And it is elementary knowledge that small homes with children to be educated in local schools cannot pay their own way tax-wise. Such municipalities, above all others, vitally need and may legally exercise comprehensive planning and implementing zoning techniques to avoid present haphazard development which can only bring future grief. They are entitled to aim thereby for a sound and balanced area, with varying uses confined to specified districts and appropriately regulated. They may even limit the pace of growth to coincide with the availability of the necessary additional facilities and services so as to minimize growing pains. See
